chunks: And what Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah (AS) from his father (AS):

that he used to fumigate the deceased with oud wood containing musk; and sometimes he would place hanut on the bier, and sometimes he would not; and he disliked that the deceased be followed by the incense burner.
The correct interpretation of these two reports is to take them as a form of taqiyya, because they are in conformity with the schools of the (Sunni) majority.

key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: taqiyya — precautionary dissimulation; acting in outward conformity with the opposing (Sunni) school to avoid harm or exposure
key_terms.الْحَنُوطَ: hanut — a mixture of camphor and aromatic substances applied to the deceased's body before shrouding; a prescribed element of Shia funeral preparation
key_terms.الْعَامَّةِ: the general public (al-'amma) — a classical Shia technical term designating the Sunni majority and their jurisprudential schools
key_terms.الْمِجْمَرَةِ: incense burner (mujmara) — a vessel for burning aromatic wood; its use in funeral processions is the subject of jurisprudential disagreement

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia ruling on fumigating the deceased with incense and placing hanut on the bier, and why does Sheikh al-Tusi classify certain hadiths on this topic as taqiyya in al-Istibsar?
ai.summary: This narration, transmitted by Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim via Imam al-Sadiq (AS) from Imam al-Baqir (AS), describes funerary practices: fumigating the deceased with musk-infused oud wood, variably placing hanut on the bier, and disapproving of an incense burner following the funeral procession. Sheikh al-Tusi appends a reconciliatory note — characteristic of al-Istibsar's methodology — instructing that these reports be interpreted as taqiyya, since they align with Sunni jurisprudential schools rather than the normative Shia position on funeral rites.
